title: Oregon Ducks QB Dante Moore Out for Remainder of 2026 Season, Says OregonLive.com
body:
Oregon’s starting quarterback, Dante Moore, will be sidelined for the remainder of the 2026 season after failing to clear the university’s concussion protocol following a hard hit during the Ducks’ September 26 clash with USC. Head coach Dan Lanning confirmed Monday night that the team does not expect Moore to return before the season concludes, a decision that reshapes the Ducks’ offensive outlook as they head into the final stretch of Pac‑12 play.

Moore’s injury occurred early in the second quarter of the Los Angeles matchup, when he absorbed a helmet‑to‑helmet collision while attempting a scramble on third down. Though he finished the game, the Ducks’ medical staff placed him in the standard concussion evaluation process, which includes a series of neurocognitive tests, symptom monitoring, and a gradual return‑to‑play protocol. After multiple assessments over the past two weeks, doctors concluded that Moore has not met the criteria for a safe return, prompting the team to make the difficult call to end his season.

The loss of Moore, who entered the year as a seasoned starter after a breakout sophomore campaign, forces Oregon to lean heavily on its depth chart. Redshirt junior quarterback Jaxon Miller, who saw limited action in the first three games, is now slated to assume the starting role. Miller brings a dual‑threat skill set, but his limited in‑game experience raises questions about how quickly he can adapt to Lanning’s fast‑paced, read‑option offense. Backup quarterback Tyler Hawkins, a true freshman with a strong arm but limited familiarity with the playbook, may also see increased snaps in specific packages, particularly in short‑yardage and goal‑line situations.

Coach Lanning addressed the situation in a press conference, emphasizing both the seriousness of concussion safety and the confidence he has in his roster. “Our priority is Dante’s health, and we’re not going to rush him back,” Lanning said. “We have a group of guys who have been working hard all season, and they’re ready to step up.” He also highlighted the importance of the offensive line’s performance in protecting the new quarterback, noting that a stronger front could mitigate the pressure Miller will now face against Pac‑12 defenses known for their aggressive pass rushes.

Analysts predict that Oregon’s offensive production may dip in the short term, especially in the passing game, where Moore’s poise and ability to extend plays were pivotal. However, the Ducks’ balanced attack—anchored by a potent running game featuring senior running back Jalen Hunt and a versatile receiving corps—offers a buffer against a prolonged slump. Defensive coordinator Pete Kelley remains optimistic, noting that a more run‑heavy approach could keep the defense rested and allow the team to stay competitive in tight conference matchups.

The broader implications for Oregon’s postseason aspirations are significant. With the Ducks currently sitting in the middle of the Pac‑12 standings, a string of victories will be essential to secure a bowl berth. The team’s next two games against Washington State and Arizona will serve as early tests of Miller’s readiness and the coaching staff’s ability to adjust schematically. If the Ducks can maintain a balanced offensive rhythm and keep turnovers low, they could still contend for a respectable bowl invitation despite the quarterback setback.

Looking ahead, Moore’s recovery timeline remains uncertain, but the medical team is optimistic that he will be cleared for spring practices, giving him a chance to rejoin the squad before the 2027 season. In the meantime, Oregon’s coaching staff faces the immediate challenge of molding a backup into a starter while preserving the team’s competitive edge. The Ducks’ resilience in the face of adversity will be measured not only by wins and losses but also by how effectively they protect their players’ long‑term health while navigating a pivotal stretch of the season.
